claims.text: Baseline inappropriate antibiotic prescribing rates were 43.5% for controls and 42.8% for clinicians randomized to the poster condition.
During the intervention period, inappropriate antibiotic prescribing rates increased to 52.7% for controls.
During the intervention period, inappropriate antibiotic prescribing rates decreased to 33.7% in the posted commitment letter condition.
Controlling for baseline prescribing rates, the posted commitment letter resulted in a 19.7 absolute percentage reduction in inappropriate antibiotic prescribing rate relative to control (P = .02).
There was no evidence of diagnostic coding shift resulting from the commitment letter intervention.
Rates of appropriate antibiotic prescriptions did not diminish over time.

evidence.description: Baseline rates were 43.5% and 42.8% for control and poster, respectively.
During the intervention period, inappropriate prescribing rates increased to 52.7% for controls.
Inappropriate prescribing rates decreased to 33.7% in the posted commitment letter condition.

Controlling for baseline prescribing rates, we found that the posted commitment letter resulted in a 19.7 absolute percentage reduction in inappropriate antibiotic prescribing rate relative to control (P = .02).
There was no evidence of diagnostic coding shift.
Rates of appropriate antibiotic prescriptions did not diminish over time.

methodologies.name: Randomized clinical trial of posted commitment letters
methodologies.description: Clinicians were randomized to display poster-sized public commitment letters in examination rooms for 12 weeks or to standard practice control to evaluate rates of inappropriate antibiotic prescribing for acute respiratory infections.
datasets: 954 adult acute respiratory infection visits across 5 outpatient primary care clinics
conditions: Posted commitment letter in examination rooms for 12 weeks

limitations.text: There have been few experiments testing nudges to improve clinical practice.
